source.title: Toy Models of Superposition
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Nicholas Schiefer; T. Henighan; S. Kravec; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; R. Lasenby; Dawn Drain; Carol Chen; R. Grosse; Sam McCandlish; J. Kaplan; D. Amodei; M. Wattenberg; Chris Olah

record.tranche_reason: The study tests superposition and polysemanticity in synthetic toy networks, using a different setup from studies of neurons in trained vision or language models.
record.gate_note: The paper's own toy-model experiments and explicit qualitative results are included. Findings it cites about real InceptionV1 or language-model neurons, and the independent replications described in comments, are not rows. Many plotted values are not available as text in the supplied study; only the textually described outcomes are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study trains small ReLU networks on synthetic sparse features and directly observes superposition and polysemantic neurons forming as sparsity rises. This is a different method aimed at V3's proposed mechanism. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors show superposition and both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons arising in toy ReLU models as features become sparse. They find this governed by phase changes, and that computation such as absolute value can occur in superposition. They argue the toy models' predictions are consistent with real-network polysemanticity. They caution that generalization to real networks is very unclear, especially for the geometry and learning-dynamics results.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small ReLU networks trained on synthetic sparse feature data, rather than interpreting neurons in trained image or language models.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported representation changes with feature sparsity, relative feature importance, feature correlations, and activation-function/model setup.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, adversarial vulnerability rises by more than 3x as superposition forms and tracks features per dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition in toy networks increases vulnerability to L2 adversarial examples.

record.problems: The paper's central experiments use synthetic toy networks, not trained real-world vision or language models. The ReLU-hidden-layer neuron visualization selects the lowest-loss result from 1000 training runs. The text does not provide uncertainty estimates or quantitative per-condition values for several plotted findings.
record.rows_left_out: Left out numerous plotted geometric configurations and learning-dynamics observations because they do not separately measure the claim's polysemanticity or its listed versions; their textual descriptions are in The Geometry of Superposition and Superposition and Learning Dynamics. Left out statements about real InceptionV1 and transformer neurons because they are prior observations or author impressions, not results of this study.

untested.parts: No measurement of image-classifier neurons. The InceptionV1 depth trend is cited prior work.
No measurement of transformer LM neurons. 'Early MLP neurons extremely polysemantic' is the authors' stated experience, not a result.
Whether superposition explains polysemantic neurons in trained real vision or language models.
Initialization, regularization or training noise as causes when capacity suffices. Only one sufficient-capacity example (n=3, m=6) is shown.
SoLU, modern convnets, MoE, and performance-preserving reductions in real models. The MoE and footnote-21 claims are speculation.
No re-examination of canonical real neurons.
The primary-versus-secondary-feature point is hypothetical ('if we were to observe the activations'). Activation ranges and scoring methods were not measured.

missing.what: With sufficient capacity (n=3, m=6), the absolute-value model learns monosemantic positive/negative neurons for each feature.
Phase diagrams (2 features in 1 dimension; 3 in 2) showing sparsity is necessary for superposition, with a first-order phase change that depends on relative importance.
Linear versus ReLU hidden layer comparison: with a ReLU activation, features align with neurons (privileged basis); with a linear hidden layer they do not.
missing.locator: Superposition in a Privileged Basis (intro figure)

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. External replications (Redwood, DeepMind, OpenAI) and Redwood's remark that activation functions change the phase diagrams are comments by others, not this study's results. The rows rightly exclude them. The V4 verdict is text-based and rests on one hand-described small model.

versions.untested_parts: No new measurements of image-classifier neurons or real visual inputs.
No new measurements of transformer language-model neurons, tokens, or contexts.
Tests the proposed mechanism in synthetic toy networks, not whether it explains polysemanticity in trained real-world networks generally.
Does not test initialization, training noise, or polysemanticity when there are enough neurons for every feature.
Does not test SoLU, modern convolutional networks, or performance-preserving reductions in real models.
Does not re-examine canonical real-model neurons with better interpretability tools or establish a shared real-world feature for their mixed responses.
The paper discusses strongest versus lower-magnitude activations in its toy model, but does not measure polysemanticity across activation ranges or compare explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: linear model
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature representation with the ReLU-output model across feature sparsity settings.
rows.measure: Number and geometry of represented features
rows.value: The model learns the top-m most important features and does not exhibit superposition.
rows.note: The paper describes this as the linear-model baseline; it says the optimized solution does not depend on sparsity.
rows.check: Control row. The linear and ReLU-output models have no privileged basis, so no neurons exist. This bears on the superposition mechanism (V3), not on the share of polysemantic neurons (V5). V5 link removed.

source_check.locator_found: Demonstrating Superposition, Basic Results (n=20, m=5, I_i=0.7^i). The Basic Results intro says the linear solution does not depend on sparsity if well optimized.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Measured learned feature representation while varying feature sparsity.
rows.measure: Number of represented features and interference between their directions
rows.baseline: Linear model learns the top-m most important features.
rows.value: The ReLU model behaves like the linear model for dense features; as sparsity increases, it represents more features non-orthogonally.
rows.note: The text describes lower-importance features entering superposition first, with more important features affected as sparsity increases.
rows.check: Non-privileged basis: shows features in superposition, not neurons. Sparsity is a data property, not architecture or training. V5 link removed.

rows.subject: ReLU output model
rows.operation_detail: Examined learned feature representation at increased model size.
rows.value: The results are described as essentially a rescaled version of the smaller model's results.
rows.note: The paper does not give numerical per-condition values in the supplied text.
rows.check: Value is only described as a rescaled version of the n=20, m=5 result. Non-privileged basis.

source_check.locator_found: Basic Results (m=20, n=80, I_i=0.9^i, 'essentially a rescaled version')

rows.subject: ReLU hidden layer model
rows.operation_detail: Examined neuron weights while varying feature sparsity.
rows.measure: Whether neurons represent one or multiple features
rows.value: Monosemantic neurons occur in some sparsity regimes, polysemantic neurons in others, and both can occur in the same model; the text describes a shift toward polysemantic neurons as sparsity increases.
rows.locator: Superposition in a Privileged Basis — Visualizing Superposition in Terms of Neurons
rows.note: For each displayed model, 1000 models were trained and the one with the lowest loss was visualized.
rows.check: Each displayed model is the lowest-loss of 1000 runs, so this is a selected solution. Neurons were labelled polysemantic by weight inspection. Varying sparsity is not an architecture or training change, so V5 link removed.

source_check.locator_found: Superposition in a Privileged Basis, Visualizing Superposition in Terms of Neurons

rows.subject: ReLU hidden layer absolute-value model
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature encoding by neurons while varying feature sparsity in a model trained to compute absolute value.
rows.measure: Neuron-feature mixtures and ability to compute the target function
rows.baseline: In the dense regime, each neuron represents a single feature.
rows.value: At sufficient sparsity, the model represents more features than neurons using superposition and usefully approximates the required computation.
rows.locator: Computation in Superposition — Superposition vs Sparsity
rows.note: The text also reports intermediate regimes with some pure-feature neurons and a subset of highly polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Neuron polysemanticity was judged by eye from weight plots. Varying sparsity is not a V5 manipulation, so V5 link removed.

source_check.locator_found: Computation in Superposition, Superposition vs Sparsity (n=100, m=40, 0.8^i)

rows.subject: toy models described in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Added an L1 penalty on hidden-layer activations.
rows.value: The paper says this can eliminate superposition, at the cost of higher loss.
rows.locator: Strategic Picture — Approach 1: Creating Models Without Superposition
rows.note: No size, λ value, loss amount, or measured performance difference is stated.
rows.check: The paper states L1 on hidden activations eliminates superposition at higher loss. No λ, model, loss values or plot are given, so it is an assertion rather than a reported measurement.

source_check.locator_found: Strategic Picture, Approach 1: Creating Models Without Superposition (add lambda*||h||_1 to the loss)
source_check.problem: The text asserts this ('quite easy', 'at the cost of a higher loss') and reports no run. The row note already says so.

rows.subject: toy models described in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Used an analytically derived attack against a random feature during adversarial training.

conditions.value: 80% of input L2 norm to fully eliminate superposition

rows.value: Adversarial training reduced superposition; attacks had to be unreasonably large (80% input L2 norm) to eliminate it fully.
rows.note: The authors say they did not explore this further.
rows.check: Superposition was reduced, but full elimination needed an attack of 80% of input L2 norm. No measured amounts or performance cost are given.

source_check.locator_found: Relationship to Adversarial Robustness, last paragraph (lines 1106-1113)

rows.subject: toy models described in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Applied analytically derived L2 adversarial examples to models as superposition formed.

conditions.value: maximum L2 attack norm of 0.1 of average input norm

rows.baseline: Vulnerability before superposition forms; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Vulnerability sharply increased by >3x and closely tracked the number of features per dimension.
rows.note: This is a consequence of superposition, not a measure named by the claim versions.
rows.check: Adversarial vulnerability is a consequence of superposition, not a version's measure. Correctly kept in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: toy model with correlated feature pairs
rows.operation_detail: Examined representations as the sparsity of three correlated feature pairs varied.

conditions.value: three pairs whose features activate together

rows.measure: Feature geometry and whether correlated features remain distinct
rows.value: In the very sparse regime, features are arranged in a hexagon with correlated features side-by-side; as sparsity decreases, features collapse into principal components, and dense-regime solutions become equivalent to PCA.
rows.locator: Superposition in a Privileged Basis — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features; Collapsing of Correlated Features
rows.note: The result shows that the representation strategy varies with sparsity and correlation.
rows.check: Hidden dimension is not stated (m=2 in this section). Non-privileged basis. The row bears on V3 only as sparsity-dependence of superposition versus PCA-like collapse.

relationships.condition: Toy ReLU networks on synthetic sparse features with more features than hidden dimensions or neurons
relationships.reason: Superposition appears only with sparsity and a nonlinearity, absent in the linear control (r1). Polysemantic neurons form as sparsity rises in privileged-basis models (r2, r3, r4, r5, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Superposition appeared only when features were sparse and the network had a nonlinearity, and the linear control showed none. In models with a privileged basis, neurons became polysemantic as sparsity increased.

source_check.condition: Toy ReLU networks on synthetic sparse features with more features than hidden dimensions or neurons
source_check.reason: Neurons turn polysemantic as sparsity rises (r4, r5), and the linear control shows no superposition (r1). r2, r3 and r9 show features in superposition, not neurons.

relationships.condition: Toy models with L1 activation regularization or adversarial training
relationships.reason: L1 regularization eliminates superposition and adversarial training reduces it, so the amount changes with regularization (r6, r7).
relationships.display_finding: L1 regularization eliminated superposition and adversarial training reduced it, so the amount of superposition depended on the regularizer.

source_check.reason: The text says L1 on hidden activations eliminates superposition and adversarial training reduces it. The L1 result is an assertion with no reported run.

relationships.condition: Same toy settings, regarding the cost of reduction
relationships.reason: L1 elimination comes with higher loss (r6). Adversarial training needs implausibly large attacks to fully eliminate superposition (r7). Reduction is not shown to be cheap.

relationships.reason: Based on text, since no row records it: with enough neurons the model learned dedicated positive and negative neurons per feature, with no polysemanticity. One example only.

tranche.reason: Different method (toy ReLU nets on synthetic sparse features) aimed at the cause of polysemanticity (V3). The study shares authors with an original.

source_check.notes: Shares authors with an original. The record's code=n is wrong: the Code section gives notebooks. r6 and r7 are brief remarks with no reported values. The Comments section reports outside replications (Redwood, McGrath, OpenAI) of the ReLU-output results only, not the neuron-level results.

statements.correction: Lowest-loss of 1000 runs: stated only for the ReLU hidden-layer n=10, m=5, 0.75^i model (r4). No selection is stated for the absolute-value n=100, m=40 model (r5). 'Judged by eye' is stated for r5. In r4, a neuron counts as polysemantic if it stores more than one feature.
statements.problem: The conditions line applies best-of-1000 selection and by-eye judging to both Toy Models settings. The text states each for only one of them.

statements.correction: Toy Models: for the n=10, m=5 ReLU hidden-layer models, 1000 models were trained per setting and the lowest-loss one is shown. The text says typical solutions are 'often similar' to these, and that selection 'reveals even more structure'. No selection is stated for the absolute-value model figures.
statements.problem: Best-of-1000 is stated only for the n=10, m=5 neuron figures, not for all neuron-level figures. The statement also leaves out the paper's caveat that typical solutions are often similar to the ones shown.

statements.correction: Code: one notebook reproduces some core diagrams and a second the theoretical phase diagrams (the Code section). The L1 and adversarial-training claims are correct as stated.
statements.problem: The 'why' line says arXiv:2209.10652 has no code. The text has a Code section with notebooks.

statements.correction: Code: notebooks reproduce some core diagrams and the theoretical phase diagrams. Adversarial training reduced superposition, and attacks of 80% of input L2 norm were needed to fully eliminate it. The n=3, m=6 V4 limit and the other numbers are correct.
statements.problem: 'code n' is wrong: the text provides notebooks. 'Adversarial training needs attacks of 80%' leaves out that 80% was needed to fully eliminate superposition; smaller attacks did reduce it.

reader_labels.condition: Synthetic toy networks with sparse features and fewer hidden dimensions than input features
reader_labels.reason: The ReLU-output and ReLU-hidden-layer experiments report extra features represented non-orthogonally and polysemantic neurons; see r2, r3, r4, and r5.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Linear versus ReLU models, and varying sparsity in toy networks
reader_labels.reason: The linear baseline does not show superposition, while ReLU models show it in sparse regimes; see r1, r2, and r4.
